chunks: Building an ideal diode. The question: How can you build an ideal diode?
An ideal diode would conduct forward with no voltage drop and block perfectly in reverse. A real diode always drops some voltage. You can get close by using other parts.
For small signals, an op-amp can hide the drop. For power, a MOSFET with a small controller acts like a diode with a drop of only millivolts.
Picture a revolving door that a helper watches. A normal diode is like a stiff one-way flap that always takes some effort to push.
The helper, the controller, senses when someone wants to enter and pushes the door open for them, and locks it the moment anyone tries to go backward.
The analogy fits closely: the helper is the control circuit, and the door is the MOSFET.
The first question to ask is signal or power.
Signal circuits use feedback to hide the diode drop; power circuits replace the diode with a MOSFET channel and add control to decide when it's on.
Forward drop: the voltage lost across a conducting diode. Op-amp: an amplifier chip with huge gain.
Wired with feedback (its output connected back to its input), it keeps correcting its output until it matches the input.
Superdiode: a diode placed inside an op-amp's feedback loop, so the op-amp cancels the drop.
MOSFET: a transistor switch turned on and off by the voltage on its control pin (the gate). R DS(on) : the small resistance of a MOSFET when it is on.
Body diode: the diode that is built into a MOSFET, pointing one way.
Take round example numbers. Say a power path carries 2 amps. A plain silicon diode drops about 0. 7 volts, so it wastes 0. 7 times 2 equals 1. 4 watts.
Now use a MOSFET with an R DS(on) of 10 milliohms and a controller that turns it on only when current should flow forward. The drop is 2 times 0. 01 equals 0.
02 volts, and the loss is about 0. 04 watts. That is the whole idea.
"For signals, an op-amp superdiode: the diode goes inside the op-amp's feedback loop, so its 0.
6 volt drop is divided by the open-loop gain and the output follows the input for positive signals, at the cost of speed.

For power, a MOSFET with a controller: the body diode points the right way, and the controller senses forward voltage and turns the gate on so the drop is just I R DS(on) , then turns it off fast if current tries to reverse.
Parts like the LTC4357 or LM74700 do this."
